content: 1. A vaccination schedule outlines the recommended vaccines for children. The text in square brackets should be adapted to include the specific country name. 2. Confidence in vaccine benefits: Parents or caregivers are asked how important they believe vaccines are for their child’s health. This question measures the percentage of parents who consider vaccines to be moderately or very important. It evaluates positive attitudes toward vaccination, emphasizing that vaccines are beneficial, essential, and valuable. Vaccines are effective in preventing diseases, saving lives, and protecting vaccinated children. 3. Confidence in vaccine safety: Parents or caregivers are asked how safe they believe vaccines are for their child. This question measures the percentage of parents who consider vaccines to be moderately or very safe. It assesses negative attitudes toward vaccination, focusing on the belief that vaccines are safe and not harmful or dangerous. 4. Confidence in health workers: Parents or caregivers are asked how much they trust the health workers who administer vaccines to children. They are given options ranging from not at all to very much. This question measures the percentage of parents who trust health workers moderately or very much. Trust in health workers reflects the belief that they are competent, reliable, and capable of providing quality healthcare. 5. Peer norms: Parents or caregivers are asked if they think most parents they know get their children vaccinated. This question measures the percentage of parents who believe that most parents in their social circle vaccinate their children. It assesses social norms and beliefs about what other parents are doing. 6. Family norms: Parents or caregivers are asked if most of their close family and friends want them to vaccinate their child. This question measures the percentage of parents who feel that their close social contacts support vaccination. It evaluates social norms and the influence of close family and friends on vaccination decisions. 7. Religious leader norms: Parents or caregivers are asked if their religious leaders want them to vaccinate their child. This question measures the percentage of parents who believe their religious leaders support vaccination. It assesses social norms and the influence of opinion leaders, such as priests, clerics, imams, or rabbis, on vaccination decisions. 8. Community leader norms: Parents or caregivers are asked if their community leaders want them to vaccinate their child. This question measures the percentage of parents who believe their community leaders support vaccination. It evaluates social norms and the influence of leaders representing neighborhoods, regions, or social groups. 9. Health worker recommendation: Parents or caregivers are asked if a health worker has recommended vaccination for their child. This question measures the percentage of parents who recall a health worker recommending vaccination. It assesses whether healthcare providers actively promote vaccination during clinic visits. 10. Received recall: Parents or caregivers are asked if they have ever been contacted about their child being due for vaccination. This question measures the percentage of parents who have been reminded about upcoming vaccinations. It evaluates the effectiveness of mechanisms in place to ensure children receive timely vaccinations. 11. Mother’s travel autonomy: Parents or caregivers are asked if the mother needs permission to take the child to the clinic for vaccination. This question measures the percentage of mothers who report not needing permission. It assesses women’s freedom to leave the home to vaccinate their child. 12. Knowledge of vaccination sites: Parents or caregivers are asked if they know where to take their child for vaccination. This question measures the percentage of parents who are aware of the location of vaccination facilities. It evaluates knowledge of the existence and location of vaccination sites. 13. Personal experience with vaccination: Parents or caregivers are asked if they have personally taken their youngest child to get vaccinated. This question measures the percentage of parents who have direct experience with vaccination clinics. It allows for analysis of those with personal interactions with clinic staff. 14. Vaccination availability: Parents or caregivers are asked if they have ever been turned away when trying to get their child vaccinated. This question measures the percentage of parents who report never being turned away. It evaluates experiences of being unable to receive vaccination due to issues such as vaccine stock-outs or clinic problems. 15. Ease of access: Parents or caregivers are asked how easy it is to access vaccination services for their child. This question measures the percentage of parents who find it moderately or very easy to access vaccination. It evaluates the general accessibility of vaccination services. 16. Affordability: Parents or caregivers are asked how easy it is to pay for vaccination, considering clinic fees, transportation costs, and time away from work. This question measures the percentage of parents who find vaccination moderately or very easy to afford. It evaluates the perceived cost of vaccination. 17. Reasons for low ease of access: Parents or caregivers are asked what makes it difficult to access vaccination services for their child. They are presented with multiple response options, such as difficulty getting to the clinic, inconvenient clinic hours, long waiting times, or being turned away. This question measures the reasons why vaccination is perceived as difficult to access. 18. Service satisfaction: Parents or caregivers are asked how satisfied they are with the vaccination services. This question measures the percentage of parents who are moderately or very satisfied. It evaluates satisfaction with the quality of services received during the last visit. 19. Service quality: Parents or caregivers are asked what aspects of the vaccination services are not satisfactory. They are presented with multiple response options, such as vaccine unavailability, long waiting times, unclean clinics, poorly trained staff, or disrespectful staff. This question measures the reasons for dissatisfaction with vaccination services.
